name: Spot the AI-productivity myth
note: Each line is something a capable engineer says in the first months of going all-in on an AI assistant. Pick the sharpest reason it fails — before an interview (or production) teaches it to you.

items.prompt: The model wrote the whole feature, it compiles, and the tests I was handed pass. That's done — shipping it.
candidates: The handed-to-you tests check the cases someone already thought of; you didn't write or read the code, so you can't say what it does on the inputs nobody tested — and 'I can't explain it' is exactly what an interviewer is probing for
Passing tests is never enough evidence to ship any code, AI-written or not
AI-written code always hides at least one bug, so it can never be trusted
You should rewrite every line the AI produced by hand before shipping it
items.correct: The handed-to-you tests check the cases someone already thought of; you didn't write or read the code, so you can't say what it does on the inputs nobody tested — and 'I can't explain it' is exactly what an interviewer is probing for
items.explanation: Comprehension and verification are still the engineer's job — the AI moved the typing, not the accountability. Passing the visible tests certifies the cases you imagined, not the system. 'Failing while the code looks fine' is the signature AI-assisted failure: it feels productive and is undefendable. The fix is reading the diff and checking it against invariants you committed up front — the next chapters.
items.principle: If you can't explain why it's correct, you haven't verified it — you've just watched it pass.

items.prompt: I ship features 5× faster with AI than I used to. That makes me a more valuable engineer.
candidates: Speed of producing code you can't defend is negative value — the bottleneck moved to judgment, review, and explanation, so 'faster output' only counts if you can still account for and gate what shipped
Measuring engineering speed is impossible, so the claim can't mean anything
AI makes every engineer exactly equally fast, so speed stopped being a differentiator
Senior engineers should never optimize for speed under any circumstances
items.correct: Speed of producing code you can't defend is negative value — the bottleneck moved to judgment, review, and explanation, so 'faster output' only counts if you can still account for and gate what shipped
items.explanation: AI commoditized code production; it did not commoditize deciding what to build, the rigor to verify it, or the communication to make it legible. Velocity without governance just produces undefendable code faster — the anti-pattern, at scale. The senior move is to pair the speed with a review-and-gate discipline so it becomes leverage, not debt.
items.principle: AI made output cheap; it made judgment, verification, and communication the scarce part.

items.prompt: The real skill now is prompt engineering. Get the prompt right and the AI handles the rest.
candidates: Prompt fluency without a committed theory is 'prompt theater' — interviewers can tell someone steering toward a spec they preregistered from someone iterating prompts until something passes
Prompts don't matter at all; any reasonable phrasing produces the same result
Prompt engineering is a fad that will disappear entirely within a year
Only the choice of model matters; the wording of the prompt is irrelevant
items.correct: Prompt fluency without a committed theory is 'prompt theater' — interviewers can tell someone steering toward a spec they preregistered from someone iterating prompts until something passes
items.explanation: The durable skill is governance over automation: clarify the problem, commit files / invariants / tests, then prompt. Prompting is one stage of the loop, not the whole job — and the strongest signal you can send is that you decided what 'right' means before you asked. Prompt-tuning until a failure hides is the opposite signal.
items.principle: Decide what 'right' means before you prompt — otherwise you're just tuning prompts until the failure hides.
